description: RapidQuake uses satellite radar observations and geospatial data to identify areas of possible earthquake damage. It creates an interactive priority map showing which districts emergency teams should inspect first. The project is led by an engineer from the Institute of Seismology of Uzbekistan and a Master's student in GIS and Technologies at TUIT.
summary:
After a strong earthquake, rescue teams face a whole damaged city and ask one question: where do we go first? Ground surveys take days, and magnitude alone does not show which districts were hit hardest. RapidQuake turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar into a ranked list of places to inspect first. We compare NISAR coherence before and after the quake, keep only built-up pixels, flag buildings whose radar signal changed strongly, and multiply that change by the number of people living there. Within minutes of a quake a first estimate comes from USGS ShakeMap × population; after the first NISAR pass it is replaced by the radar-based ranking. We tested it on the M7.4 earthquake of 10 August 2026 in Pereira, Colombia: our top-10 squares cover 20% of the built-up area but contain 52% of the buildings that Copernicus EMS mapped as damaged, and our district ranking matches theirs (Spearman ρ = 0.89, 6 comunas). For our home city, Tashkent, we pre-computed the radar "normal": NISAR can reliably watch 78% of buildings in all 12 districts, so the city is ready before the next quake.

details:
What it does. RapidQuake is a priority map for emergency teams. It answers "where do we go first?" in the first days after an earthquake, using free NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data that sees through clouds, day and night.

How it works.

1. Normal. From NISAR L2 GUNW coherence (20 m) of the 12-day pairs before the event we compute each pixel's normal coherence and its natural spread.

2. Change. For the pair spanning the earthquake we compute the drop from normal. That pair is 24 days long, so we subtract the city-wide drop and keep only the extra change.

3. Buildings only. An OpenStreetMap building mask removes trees, fields and water. A drop above 0.15 (about two times the normal spread) is flagged as possible damage. Ascending and descending orbits (tracks 47 and 11) are averaged.

4. Priority. For equal 500 m squares and for districts: share of flagged buildings × population (WorldPop). Squares with few buildings are pulled toward the city average so one noisy pixel cannot reach the top.

5. Two stages. Stage 0, minutes after the quake: USGS ShakeMap intensity × population. Stage 1, after the first NISAR pass (3 days in Pereira): the radar ranking replaces it.

Validation (Pereira, M7.4, 10 Aug 2026). Checked against the Copernicus EMS EMSR916 damage map, which was made independently from optical imagery: the top-10 squares hold 20% of the built-up area but 52% of destroyed and damaged buildings; flagged pixels occur 5.5× more often under damaged buildings than under random ones; Spearman ρ = 0.66 over 39 squares and 0.89 over 6 comunas (p = 0.02). The result holds for thresholds 0.10–0.20.

Tashkent. We processed the full city from NISAR track 84 (three pairs, June–July 2026). 78% of the built-up area has stable, high coherence, so a Pereira-like change would be visible; every district is between 72% and 85%. Because WorldPop underestimates Tashkent, we use official 2025 population from the Tashkent City Statistics Department, combined with building share into an exposure index per district.

Benefits and impact. Free open data, whole city in one pass, through clouds, about two minutes of processing. A short, ranked list that a crisis centre can act on, instead of a picture to interpret. Built for Uzbekistan's emergency services, local governments and humanitarian organizations, and transferable to any city NISAR covers.

Tools. Python (h5py, rasterio, GDAL, NumPy, geopandas, osmnx, asf_search, matplotlib), QGIS for district maps and layouts, Leaflet / HTML / CSS / JavaScript for the web app, GitHub Pages for hosting, WSL Ubuntu.

Creativity. The Pereira quake was about 100 km deep, so the ground barely moved but buildings fell. Instead of InSAR displacement we used coherence, and we corrected the longer co-event pair by subtracting the city-wide drop. We also pre-compute a "readiness" map for a city before any quake happens.

What we considered. Red means possible damage: radar cannot tell a crack from a collapse, and construction can cause false alarms, so the output is an inspection list, not a verdict. Population data quality (official statistics instead of WorldPop in Tashkent). Orbit revisit and the delay of the first pass. A simple interface for non-specialists. Honest validation against an independent reference.

How it was made. The NASA data were downloaded before the event, as the local organizers asked, and the processing scripts were drafted and tested then. During the hackathon the team re-ran the whole chain from raw NISAR files, processed the full city of Tashkent, built the web app, the QGIS maps, the slides and the video. An AI coding assistant helped write the Python code and draft texts; the team chose the data and method, ran every step and checked the results.
